lesson.title: or: True When At Least One Side Is
lesson.summary: The or operator combines two boolean expressions and evaluates to True whenever at least one of them is True, capturing situations where any single qualifying condition is enough.
lesson.body:
or takes two boolean expressions and evaluates to True as long as at least one side is True. The only case where or produces False is when both sides are False; every other combination, both True, or exactly one True, results in True. This matches the everyday sense of "either one is fine." A store might announce that seniors or students get a discount, meaning a customer only needs to satisfy one of those two conditions, not both, to qualify.

This is worth contrasting directly with and, which was covered in the previous section. and demands that every side hold; or only demands that some side holds. Choosing between them is really a choice about how strict a requirement should be, and getting it backwards is a genuine and common source of logic bugs, especially because English sometimes uses "or" ambiguously in ways code cannot afford to be ambiguous about.

Trace this eligibility check:

is_member = False
has_coupon = True
gets_discount = is_member or has_coupon
print(gets_discount)

Python evaluates is_member, which is False, and has_coupon, which is True. or combines these: since at least one side, has_coupon, is True, the whole expression evaluates to True regardless of what is_member holds. gets_discount is bound to True. If both is_member and has_coupon had been False, or would have evaluated to False as well, since neither condition would have been satisfied.

It is worth being precise about what kind of "or" this is. In everyday speech, "or" sometimes means exactly one of two options, as in choosing soup or salad, implying not both. Python's or is never that kind; it is what logicians call an inclusive or, meaning it is perfectly happy to be True when both sides are True as well. If is_member and has_coupon were both True in the example above, gets_discount would still evaluate to True, not to some special result for having too many qualifying conditions. When a program genuinely needs an exclusive or, meaning exactly one side but not both, it has to be built explicitly out of and, or, and not rather than relying on or by itself.

Like and, or is not limited to two operands; Python allows longer chains such as a or b or c, evaluating as though written (a or b) or c, and the whole expression is True as soon as any single piece is True. A widely used idiom builds on this same idea to supply default values: display_name = nickname or username or "Guest" picks whichever of the three values is the first one that counts as satisfying, falling back to "Guest" only if neither nickname nor username is available. This idiom actually leans on truthiness rather than strict boolean values, a connection this chapter explores in detail in the section on truthiness and falsiness.

When or is combined with and in the same expression, remember that and binds more tightly, so a or b and c groups as a or (b and c) rather than (a or b) and c. Adding explicit parentheses whenever both operators appear together in one line keeps the intended grouping unambiguous to any reader, rather than relying on everyone remembering the precedence rules correctly.
